historical_timeline.summary: Her mother dies after a long illness.
Her elder sisters Maria and Elizabeth die.
Jane Eyre published under the name Currer Bell.
Her brother Branwell and her sister Emily die.
Her sister Anne dies of tuberculosis.
Lingering cold and sore throat after a walk in the rain.
Onset of perpetual nausea and faintness.
Writes that she has been confined to bed for three weeks; the household servant dies about this time.
Low wandering delirium; she asks for food.
Dies at Haworth; the death certificate gives phthisis, and other causes are proposed later.

claims.statement: Charlotte Brontë was born on 21 April 1816 in Thornton, Yorkshire, the third of six children of Maria Branwell and her husband, an Anglican clergyman.
Jane Eyre was first published in 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell.
Her mother died on 15 September 1821, in the 39th year of her age, after a long and painful illness.
Her mother's illness may have been cancer; one reference work says uterine cancer. The cause is a later interpretation.

Her two elder sisters, Maria and Elizabeth, fell ill at the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge and died at home in 1825, Maria on 6 May aged 11 and Elizabeth on 15 June aged 10; reference works give tuberculosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The causes are as given by the reference works; the school also had an outbreak of typhus.

claims.statement: Her brother Branwell died on 24 September 1848, aged 31, of several conditions made worse by heavy drinking; tuberculosis is listed among them.
Her sisters Emily and Anne died of tuberculosis, Emily on 19 December 1848 aged 30 and Anne on 28 May 1849 aged 29.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Household tuberculosis deaths; the reason for tuberculosis screening in the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: On 29 June 1854 she married Arthur Bell Nicholls, her father's curate, at Haworth.
In late November 1854, after a long walk on the moors to a waterfall that ended in heavy rain, she began to shiver and had a bad lingering sore throat and cold that made her thin and weak.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An intercurrent illness before the final one, in Gaskell's account.

claims.statement: Early in 1855, after a visit to Gawthorpe and a long walk over damp ground in thin shoes, she was attacked by "new sensations of perpetual nausea, and ever-recurring faintness"; a doctor who was called assigned a natural cause for her indisposition.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The onset of the final illness, in Gaskell's account.

claims.statement: The sickness increased until the very sight of food caused nausea. On 15 February 1855 she wrote that she had been confined to bed for three weeks, that up to then she had had excellent health since her marriage, and that she was much reduced and very weak.
Tabitha Ackroyd, the family's elderly servant, died during Charlotte's illness; a literary historian writes that she died of a digestive infection six weeks before Charlotte.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context for the infectious explanations in CLM-0018.

claims.statement: About the third week of March 1855 a low wandering delirium came on, in which she begged constantly for food; she died early on Saturday 31 March 1855 at Haworth, in the 39th year of her age.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: Her death certificate gave the cause of death as phthisis, a term for pulmonary tuberculosis.

She is widely reported to have been in the early stages of pregnancy when she died; Gaskell records that her servant cheered her with the thought of the baby that was coming, and a letter of hers suggests that she was pregnant. The death certificate does not mention pregnancy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic first pregnancy.

claims.statement: Hyperemesis gravidarum has been proposed as the cause of her final illness and death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective diagnosis; the synthetic episode teaches its modern management without asserting it as her diagnosis.

claims.statement: A 2019 clinical nutrition paper agrees that hyperemesis gravidarum is the most likely diagnosis and suggests that the refeeding syndrome, after her appetite returned in the third week of March, caused her death; it argues there is no more than circumstantial evidence for tuberculosis and that Addison's disease fits poorly.
A bacterial infection such as typhoid has also been suggested, possibly caught from the servant who died weeks earlier.
A 1991 obstetrics paper doubts that she was ever pregnant and argues that tuberculosis with secondary Addison disease explains her terminal illness.

Tuberculosis as the cause of her death, as the death certificate records, is disputed; the diagnosis was made without modern tests, and later writers have proposed hyperemesis gravidarum, refeeding syndrome, typhoid, and Addison disease instead.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The diagnostic conflict is recorded, not resolved.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Prenatal care of a first pregnancy at 38 complicated by hyperemesis gravidarum, following ACOG Practice Bulletin 189 and RCOG Green-top Guideline 69 (2024): dating ultrasound; severity by the PUQE-24 score, weight, and hydration rather than urine ketones; electrolytes, magnesium, phosphate, liver tests, and thyroid tests with recognition of gestational transient thyrotoxicosis; stepwise antiemetics (doxylamine-pyridoxine, then metoclopramide, then ondansetron after counseling on the very small absolute risk of orofacial clefting); admission with intravenous saline and potassium, thiamine before any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, magnesium replacement, refeeding precautions, and weight-adjusted thromboprophylaxis; mental health screening with the PHQ-9 and EPDS; routine prenatal care at an advanced maternal age, with aneuploidy screening offered (cell-free DNA and nuchal translucency, with diagnostic testing available), low-dose aspirin for two moderate preeclampsia risk factors, and tuberculosis screening with an interferon-gamma release assay because of tuberculosis deaths in her household. The historical cause of her death is disputed and is recorded as conflicting retrospective claims, not decided by the modern episode.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Brontë returns one week after starting doxylamine-pyridoxine, two tablets at bedtime, at 8 weeks 1 day. The bedtime dose helps her sleep, but nausea lasts most of the day and she now vomits four or five times a day. She keeps down small amounts of water, tea, and dry crackers most days and passes urine normally. She feels lightheaded only when she gets up quickly. She has stopped writing and lies down most of the afternoon. She has had no pain, bleeding, fever, or diarrhea. Her PUQE-24 score is 11 (moderate), up from 10. She weighs 44.0 kg, 4.3 percent below her pre-pregnancy weight. She saw Dr. Oyelaran-Hughes of maternal-fetal medicine this morning.
